scenarios.name: Teams are NS for seats 1 and 3 and EW for seats 2 and 4
Deal gives 7 cards to each seat and 2 to the kitty (random deal, counts only)
In hand 2 seat 2 declares and names trumps
In hand 3 seat 3 declares and names trumps
In hand 4 seat 4 declares and names trumps
Declarer seat 1 names Diamonds as trumps in hand 1, and only the declarer is asked
Jokers and trump-suit cards form one Trump suit for following
A non-trump lead sets led suit to that suit; trump-suit cards do not follow it
Leading a trump-suit card sets led suit to Trump, so jokers must follow
A follower with no led-suit card is offered every card; a follower with one is offered only led-suit cards
Play goes anticlockwise from leader seat 3 and later seats follow the led suit
A low trump beats the led suit's ace and king; an off-suit card is weakest
Big Joker beats Small Joker, which beats the trump ace
The trick winner's team takes the points and the winner leads the next trick
The kitty's points go to the winner of the last trick (EW 5 + kitty 15 = 20)
Defenders on 15 points: the declaring team NS gains 3 match points
Defenders NS on 30 points: the declaring team EW gains 2 match points
Defenders EW on 50 points: the defending team gains 1 match point
Defenders NS on 60 points: the defending team gains 2 match points
Defenders EW on 85 points: the defending team gains 3 match points
Hand points add to the running card-point totals and reset to 0 when the next hand starts
After hand 4 the team with more match points (NS) wins
Match points level after hand 4: the team with more card points (EW) wins
Match points and card points both level after hand 4: all four seats share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed two partnerships of two. Fewer seats break the teams, and more seats do not fit the 30-card deal of 7 each plus a 2-card kitty.

The rules forbid talk; signalling through card play is the skill. A thoughtful player tracks played trumps and points, smears points onto a partner's winning trick, and holds trumps back to capture kings and tens.

spec_choices.what: Team scores are mirrored onto each player's match_points and card_points
spec_choices.why: The ranking expression works per player, so both partners carry the team's totals.
Card points can total at most 400, so match points always come first and card points break ties. A full tie makes all four seats share the win, which is the draw.
The rules do not say how cards are labelled; codes let suit, rank and points be read arithmetically.

simplifications.what: The 32 rounds run as one repeated step list, with `when` conditions on round_in_hand choosing the deal steps (round 1) or the trick steps (rounds 2 to 8)
simplifications.why: The step list is flat; a condition on each single step gives the same order.

simplifications.what: Legality of following suit is enforced by offering only legal cards, with a judged check as a backstop
simplifications.why: The source rejects illegal plays and asks again; offering only legal cards has the same effect.

simplifications.what: A draw is shown as all four seats sharing the win
simplifications.why: The engine has no separate draw outcome.

variation.original_summary: Da Bai Fen is a four-player partnership trick-taking game of the Sheng Ji / Tractor family. Trumps are declared during the deal, the leader buries a kitty, and multi-card leads are allowed. Teams fight over 100 points in point cards, and that total decides whether the declarers keep the lead and climb levels.

review.evidence: No simple card-play policy wins. 'Always play your highest card' wastes trumps and gives point cards to opponents. 'Always play lowest' never captures. Seat order matters, but the declarer role moves between teams.

Over many deals, good card play wins clearly. In a short session the deal decides a lot: trump length, jokers and kitty contents. The voluntary race to expose a trump card also turns partly on the order of the deal.
There is much to master: counting trumps, inferring voids, partnership signalling through discards, and timing point cards. A weak player can still win tricks with strong cards.
Hands and kitty are hidden. Players must infer holdings from follows and discards, model the partner's intentions, and plan trump control over a whole hand.
Trick winners and point totals follow from card ranks. The level outcome is a table lookup on points.

Several rules exceed the engine limits: card-by-card dealing with interruptible trump exposure, kitty exchange, multi-card leads with a legality check against all hidden hands, and void-hand redeals. A 54-card, 12-trick deal with a level race from 2 to Ace is far too long and has too many steps.

problems: Trump declaration during a one-by-one deal, where any holder may interrupt, is a real-time-like race that the engine cannot run in a few steps.
Multi-card leads require checking that no card in any hidden hand beats them; this is a long, error-prone rule chain.
The kitty exchange (take 6, discard 6) and void-hand redeals add choice steps and conditional blocks the flat step list cannot support.
54 cards, 12 tricks per deal and a level race from 2 to Ace make the game far too long for the 40-round cap.
A short session is dominated by deal luck (jokers, trump length), and the declaring role does not rotate evenly, so one team can gain a structural edge.

changes.what: The deck shrinks to 30 cards: four suits of 5, 8, 10, J, Q, K, A plus two jokers. Each player gets 7 cards and 2 go to a face-down kitty. Point cards stay K=10, 10=10, 5=5, still 100 in total.
changes.why: Keeps the 100-point fight while making each deal 7 tricks long.
changes.fixes: 54 cards, 12 tricks per deal and a level race from 2 to Ace make the game far too long for the 40-round cap.

changes.what: There is no level system or trump rank. Trumps are the two jokers plus a trump suit that the hand's declarer names after seeing their own 7 cards.
changes.why: One single choice step replaces the interruptible exposure race. The declarer still reads their hand to choose trumps, as in the original.
changes.fixes: Trump declaration during a one-by-one deal, where any holder may interrupt, is a real-time-like race that the engine cannot run in a few steps.

changes.what: Only single-card leads are allowed. A player must follow suit if able, and trumps count as their own suit.
changes.why: Removes the multi-card legality check while keeping follow-suit inference and the value of being void in a suit.
changes.fixes: Multi-card leads require checking that no card in any hidden hand beats them; this is a long, error-prone rule chain.

changes.what: The kitty is never exchanged. Its points go to whichever team wins the last trick, and its cards are revealed only then. There are no redeals.
changes.why: Keeps a hidden element and a reason to fight for the last trick, without extra choice steps.
changes.fixes: The kitty exchange (take 6, discard 6) and void-hand redeals add choice steps and conditional blocks the flat step list cannot support.

changes.what: The match has 4 hands. The declarer rotates through all four seats, so each team declares twice. Each hand pays match points from a threshold table on the defenders' points. The higher match total wins, with card points as the tie-break.
changes.why: Balances the seats and spreads deal luck over four deals. The threshold table keeps the original's stay-or-flip character on the 40-point line.
changes.fixes: A short session is dominated by deal luck (jokers, trump length), and the declaring role does not rotate evenly, so one team can gain a structural edge.

changes.what: The winning card in each trick is decided by a numeric strength: rank, plus 10 if the card is in the led suit, plus 20 if it is a trump. The jokers have fixed top values.
changes.why: Lets the engine find the trick winner in one calculation step with no lookup table.
changes.fixes: 54 cards, 12 tricks per deal and a level race from 2 to Ace make the game far too long for the 40-round cap.

keeps: Four players in fixed facing partnerships.
Point cards K=10, 10=10, 5=5 totalling 100, with the 40-point line deciding whether declarers or defenders profit.
Two jokers as the top trumps (red/big above black/small), and a trump suit chosen from the declarer's hand.
A hidden kitty whose points matter at the end of the hand.
Follow-suit trick play, anticlockwise order, and trick winners leading the next trick.
Partnership inference and signalling purely through which cards are played.

recommendation.reason: Trick-taking with hidden hands, partner modelling and point management is strong reasoning material. The parts that break the limits (exposure race, multi-card leads, kitty exchange, levels) can be cut while keeping the 100-point partnership core.

variation.name: Da Bai Fen Lite
variation.summary: Four players in two facing partnerships play four short hands of single-card trick-taking. In each hand a declarer names trumps and the defenders try to capture 40 of the 100 points in play. The declarer role rotates so each team declares twice.
variation.rules:
SEATS AND TEAMS. Seats 1, 2, 3 and 4 sit in anticlockwise order. Seats 1 and 3 are Team North-South (NS). Seats 2 and 4 are Team East-West (EW). Partners cannot see each other's cards. There is no talk; the only communication is the cards played.

DECK. The deck has 30 cards. Each of four suits (Spades, Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds) has seven cards: 5, 8, 10, J, Q, K, A, with rank values 5=1, 8=2, 10=3, J=4, Q=5, K=6, A=7. There are also two jokers: the Big Joker and the Small Joker. Point cards: each K is worth 10 points, each 10 is worth 10 points, each 5 is worth 5 points. All other cards and both jokers are worth 0. The deck holds 100 points in total.

MATCH STRUCTURE. The match has 4 hands of 8 rounds each, 32 rounds in total. The declarer is seat 1 in hand 1, seat 2 in hand 2, seat 3 in hand 3 and seat 4 in hand 4. The declarer's team is the Declaring Team for that hand; the other team is the Defending Team.

ROUND 1 OF EACH HAND (DEAL AND TRUMPS). The 30 cards are shuffled (the only random draw of the round). Each player privately receives 7 cards. The remaining 2 cards form the face-down kitty, which no one sees. The declarer then names one suit as the trump suit, and it is announced to all. Trumps are the Big Joker, the Small Joker and the 7 cards of the trump suit, 9 cards in all. For following purposes all trumps form one suit, the Trump suit. The declarer will lead the first trick.

ROUNDS 2 TO 8 OF EACH HAND (ONE TRICK EACH).
(a) The leader plays any one card face up. The suit of that card is the led suit; if the card is a trump, the led suit is Trump.
(b) The other three players then each play one card face up, one after another, in anticlockwise order from the leader. Each sees the cards already played. A player holding a card of the led suit must play one. A player holding none may play any card. An illegal play is rejected and the player must choose again.
(c) Strength of each played card. Big Joker = 40. Small Joker = 39. A trump-suit card = 20 + its rank value. A non-trump card of the led suit = 10 + its rank value. Any other card = its rank value.
(d) The card with the highest strength wins the trick. Ties cannot occur. The winner's team adds the point values of the four cards to its hand points, and the winner leads the next trick.
(e) In round 8 (the 7th and last trick), the kitty is also revealed after the trick, and its points are added to the hand points of the team that won that trick.

END OF HAND SCORING. Let P be the Defending Team's hand points, always a multiple of 5 from 0 to 100.
- P from 0 to 15: Declaring Team +3 match points.
- P from 20 to 35: Declaring Team +2.
- P from 40 to 55: Defending Team +1.
- P from 60 to 75: Defending Team +2.
- P from 80 to 100: Defending Team +3.
In addition, each team adds its hand points to its running card-point total. Hand points then reset to 0 for the next hand.
variation.objective: After hand 4, the team with more match points wins, and both its players win. If match points are equal, the team with the higher card-point total over all four hands wins. If that is also equal, the match is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Play becomes a compact trick-taking duel. Strong play counts trumps (9 per hand), infers voids from failures to follow, protects or feeds point cards to the partner when the partner is winning the trick, and plans for the last trick and its hidden kitty. The trump choice rewards reading one's own hand: a long suit versus spreading the risk across suits. Rotating the declarer gives each team two declaring hands and each seat one, so no seat has a built-in edge, and four deals reduce card luck. The match-point bands cap the reward for one lucky deal, so consistent play across hands matters most. Simple policies lose: 'always highest legal card' burns trumps early and loses the last trick and kitty; 'always lowest' concedes points; 'always lead points' feeds the opponents. Talk is left out on purpose. Any message would be public, so it either reveals hands to opponents or adds noise. The partnership-inference challenge is to read the partner's cards from play alone.

balanced.evidence:
DECK ARITHMETIC. 4 suits x 7 = 28 cards, plus 2 jokers = 30. Points per suit are K 10 + 10 10 + 5 5 = 25, so 4 x 25 = 100. Deal: 4 x 7 = 28 cards in hands plus a 2-card kitty = 30. Seven tricks use 7 x 4 = 28 cards. All consistent.

STRENGTH TABLE (c). Jokers are 40 and 39. Trump-suit cards are 21 to 27. Led-suit cards are 11 to 17. Off-suit cards are 1 to 7. Off-suit cards can tie with each other, but the led card itself is at least 11, so an off-suit card is never highest. The 'no ties' claim holds.

SEAT AND MOVE-ORDER EDGE. The declarer sees 7 cards, names trumps and leads first. Rough estimate: the declarer's best suit plus a share of the jokers gives about 3 to 3.5 trumps. The partner holds about 7/23 of the remaining trumps, roughly 1.6. So the declaring side holds about 5 of the 9 trumps, the defenders about 3.5, and the kitty about 0.4. Declarers might expect about 55 to 60 card points, leaving P around 40 to 45.

HAND-SCORE BANDS by P (defenders' points):
- 0 to 15: Declarers +3
- 20 to 35: Declarers +2
- 40 to 55: Defenders +1
- 60 to 75: Defenders +2
- 80 to 100: Defenders +3
The bands lean toward the defenders, which offsets the declarer's advantage, much as in the original game. Seats 1 to 4 each declare once, so NS and EW each declare twice. The match is structurally symmetric between teams.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the WINNER RULE (team match points, then card points):
- Always play the highest-strength legal card: spends jokers and trumps on pointless tricks, gives up control late, and feeds points into tricks the opponents later win. Against sensible play it loses most hands, so it loses the match.
- Always play the first (or the lowest) legal card: never contests point-rich tricks. Sensible opponents win them, P lands in the bands against this team, and it loses.
- Always name the longest suit as trump and lead it: reasonable as a heuristic, but it is not dominant. Following and discarding decisions still decide the point flow.
No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does. Results depend on the joint card distribution and on play.

CAN BOTH WIN. Yes. Each team declares twice, and every band is reachable. Card points always sum to 400 across both teams, so an exact tie needs 200 to 200 together with equal match points. Draws are rare. There is no labelled payoff ordering to contradict.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS. All of the following are fully specified:
- seats, teams and anticlockwise order
- deck, ranks and point values
- deal (7 each, 2 in the kitty, kitty unseen)
- trump naming by the fixed declarer of each hand
- the 'Trump suit' rule for following, with jokers belonging to it
- the follow-suit obligation and rejection of illegal plays
- the numeric strength formula, so the trick winner is pure arithmetic
- the leader of each trick
- the kitty going to the winner of the last trick
- the band table, the card-point tiebreak and the draw case
There is no situation without a rule.

FINITENESS AND ARITHMETIC. Exactly 4 x 8 = 32 rounds. The winner comes from match points, then card points, all kept by the game. No judge, board or clock is needed.

LIMITS. The stated values fit every limit:
- 32 rounds, limit 40
- 16 steps per round, limit 20
- 4 choice steps, limit 4 (one choice in deal rounds: trump naming; four in trick rounds: the four card plays)
- 18 attributes, limit 20
- 1 random draw per round, the shuffle in round 1 of each hand only, limit 1
- 2 hidden element types (private hands and the kitty), limit 3

ENGINE CAPABILITIES. The deal is shared_deck_draw via remove/append, a supported workaround. Deal rounds and trick rounds differ only through per-step `when` conditions on the round number within the hand. That is per-step conditioning, not a swapped block, so it is allowed. Card plays are sequential_choice, which the engine supports, and turn order is the point of trick play, so a simultaneous poll is not required. Strength and winner are single arithmetic steps with `if` operations. There is no trading, no binding agreement and no real time.

TALK. Players are on fixed teams, opposed teams want opposite outcomes, and partners share one outcome. Free talk between partners would simply leak hands and remove the inference. Omitting talk and leaving the cards as the only signals is the sensible choice.

LATE-ROUND BETRAYAL TEST. Not applicable. This is not a cooperate/defect dilemma; each trick is a contest over points.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SKILLS THAT MATTER:
- choosing the trump suit from a 7-card hand
- counting the 9 trumps and the 100 points as they fall
- inferring voids from discards
- inferring the partner's holding from their plays, since no talk is allowed
- deciding when to lead trumps to draw them
- feeding K, 10 and 5 into tricks the partner is winning
- holding trump control for the last trick, which also wins the kitty (up to 20 points)
Hidden information is present: four private hands and the kitty. Players can act on it through lead, follow and discard choices.

LUCK ESTIMATE. Four independent deals and no duplicate structure. Hand strength, trump length and joker location matter substantially. I estimate chance at about 40 to 50 percent of the outcome between equally skilled teams. The kitty's 0 to 20 points can swing a band, but they go to the winner of the last trick, which play decides.

ALL PLAYERS USING GOOD STRATEGY. The result then depends on the deals, but not on a single hidden draw alone. Each team declares twice, so trump choice and lead advantage are shared. The bands give the weaker side of a deal room to limit damage: holding the defenders below 40, or the declarers under the threshold, is a play decision. Between a reasoning team and a careless team (one that wastes trumps, feeds points to the opponents and fails to track voids), the 7-trick, 100-point structure gives the reasoning team a clear edge across 28 tricks. Chance does not alone decide most matches.

design_flags_left: every random match ended 'seats 1 and 3': choices do not change the result
the built game has 5 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4

triage.reason: The game was built as specified, and evaluation found design flaws. Because the step list is flat, the declarer's trump-naming choice sits beside the four card plays and gives 5 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4. Every random match also ended as a win for seats 1 and 3, so the players' choices do not change the result.
triage.guidance: Bring each round down to at most 4 choice steps by removing the separate trump-naming decision. Either fix the trump suit by hand number (hand 1 Spades, hand 2 Hearts, hand 3 Clubs, hand 4 Diamonds), or make the trump suit the suit of the declarer's first lead, so naming trumps is part of a play the declarer already makes. Then rework the balance so card play actually decides matches. Make sure the deal is a real fresh random draw each hand, not a fixed order that hands NS the same strong cards every time. Rotate the leader and declarer so neither team gets a structural edge from leading first or declaring in hands 1 and 3. Check that the score bands are not tilted toward NS. A shorter design is also worth considering, for example fewer hands, or tricks with fewer forced follow-suit plays, so that playing well and playing randomly lead to clearly different results.
